preference_rationale:
Both are defensible depending on how strong the retail claim needs to be, which is why this stays weak. Ultimately the point is to understand whether round lots are profitable to trade against; proving statistically that they are retail is a secondary goal. A treats it as secondary and tests it inside the pipeline; B makes it a hard gate and can die on it.

There is no strict order-level disclosure of retail versus institutional to a market maker - on lit venues orders arrive anonymized, and the only genuine tag is a Retail Liquidity Program flag, which has near-perfect precision but very low recall. B accepts this and triangulates imperfect public labels. But this firm internalizes retail flow, so it holds proprietary ground truth on its own book that no outside researcher has, and neither plan reaches for it. That makes B's five-gate apparatus a solution to a data problem this particular firm does not have.

The mechanism and broad-market readings are both partially right, but the payoff question is the primary one. It stays weak because adverse selection is this firm's central risk, and there is a real argument that knowing what you are quoting against matters more here than it would to a daily long-short book.
why_loser_was_defensible: A more conservative firm would take method B's view, wanting more confidence that round lots are connected to dumb money before deciding whether they are profitable to trade against. A more aggressive firm lets the P&L speak, does not much care whether the flow is retail, and takes on the adverse-selection risk. Which is right depends on how strong the retail claim needs to be, and that is a question about firm posture rather than about method. For a market maker the conservative reading has real force, since quoting into informed flow you had labelled uninformed is precisely the way this business loses money.
